title: Remaining Human-Centered in the Age of AI
author: Teaching in the Age of AI
summary: A high school teacher begins with an ordinary Thursday evening in which he, his daughter and their devices moved through AI, voice assistants and school software without a second thought, to argue that smart technology is now ambient. He worries that the recent turn against screens and AI in schools, including New York City's one-year moratorium on student-facing generative AI through eighth grade, will overcorrect toward bans. Citing Jenny Anderson, he says schools must work out what to protect and how to prepare students, and do both in a way parents can see and believe in. His own survey of students found that all used AI for schoolwork, that nearly ninety percent did not want to depend on it, and that many asked for instruction on using it well. He concludes that restrictions can protect learning but cannot replace teaching AI literacy, and he borrows from Pope Leo XIV the idea that students must learn when and for what purpose AI ought not to be used. Most schools have rules about AI, he notes, but very few have a curriculum.
points: Smart technology has become ambient, so avoiding AI now takes active effort and a technology-free school bubble is not realistic.
New York City's moratorium on student-facing generative AI shows the risk of overcorrecting toward bans while requiring AI literacy only in high school.
The author's student survey found universal AI use for schoolwork, a strong aversion to dependence, and a request for instruction on using AI to learn rather than get answers.
Schools need to teach digital and media literacy that includes AI, protecting students' initial thinking while showing where AI feedback helps.
Most schools have AI rules but very few have an AI curriculum, which leaves the conversation to individual teachers.
quotes: AI is already an environment in which we are immersed, as well as a force with which we must engage.
Smart technology is now ambient. At this point, if you don’t want to use or be exposed to AI, you have to actively avoid many of the ways it’s already seeped into our lives.
The problem is that the gulf between what’s possible with AI in schools and the national conversation around it makes it likely that we will overcorrect toward bans.

The actual task in front of schools is harder and less satisfying than a black-and-white policy. It’s this: Figuring out what to protect and how to prepare, and doing both in a way parents can see and believe in.

Producing an essay is not the main purpose of writing one. Sitting with a thought, spinning it out in different directions, and reworking it until it’s clear enough to be understood by someone else is a lifelong practice.
Restrictions can protect learning, but Anderson is right that they cannot substitute for teaching students to understand AI.
Educating people about the use of AI, then, involves teaching them to decide when and for what purpose it ought not to be used.
Most of the schools I know have rules about AI by now. Very few have a curriculum.
